analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal law requiring prevailing union-scale wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: A bill by 13 Republican senators to repeal the federal prevailing-wage law for construction workers was referred to a Senate committee and never received any vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1931, the Davis-Bacon Act has required companies working on federally funded construction to pay workers the wages that prevail locally for their trade — usually union-scale pay. This bill would erase that requirement entirely. Its backers said that would save the government money on construction contracts and open bidding to more small contractors. Construction workers on federal jobs would no longer have a legal wage floor, and contractors could win bids by paying less than the local standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, if the promised savings on construction contracts materialize, and nonunion or lower-wage contractors who could win federal bids by paying workers below the local prevailing rate. Opponents argued contractors who pay less would gain at their workers' expense.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931, which requires contractors on federally financed construction to pay laborers and mechanics the locally prevailing wage for their class of work [S2].

The bill's stated goals are 'new job opportunities,' 'significant cost savings on Federal construction contracts,' 'small business participation in Federal contracting,' and reduced paperwork and reporting requirements [S3].
Removing the wage floor would let contractors bid lower on federal construction projects, since labor costs would no longer be set at local prevailing rates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects, who would lose the requirement that they be paid local prevailing wages — in practice often union-scale pay — for their trade. Workers in areas where prevailing rates were set by union contracts stood to see the largest cuts.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the only federal guarantee that workers on federal construction jobs earn local prevailing wages, allowing contractors to cut pay below union-scale rates to win bids [S2].

Supporters of prevailing-wage rules have long argued that cutting wages on public works does not save money overall but shifts costs from contractors to workers through lower pay and benefits, and can pull down wage standards in the local construction market more broadly (general knowledge of the debate; not from the provided sources).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings promised to taxpayers would come directly out of construction workers' paychecks, since the wage floor is the mechanism being repealed. Whether repeal would actually lower total project costs, or simply redistribute them from labor to contractor profits, is the central dispute over Davis-Bacon and is not resolved in the bill's materials.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never took it up, so it died when this Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Hank Brown of Colorado introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on July 14, 1993, joined on introduction by eight other Republican senators [S3].
Twelve senators signed on as cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action is recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects kept the prevailing-wage requirement, and unionized contractors kept the protection of bidding against rivals who must pay the same wage floor. Taxpayers did not get the construction savings the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal construction workers and union contractors

for.name: Sen. Hank Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act and delivered introductory remarks

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote

against.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee holding the bill, never brought it to a markup or vote

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic-led Senate committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: Repeal would let these contractors win federal bids by paying below local prevailing wages instead of matching union-scale rates. Their gain comes directly from cutting the pay of workers on public projects.
Davis-Bacon prevents rivals from undercutting union-scale bids by paying less. Without it, these firms would face lower-wage competition on federal work.

industries.industry: Building trades unions and federal construction workers
industries.note: The wage floor that keeps pay on federal projects at locally prevailing — typically union — rates would disappear, putting downward pressure on members' wages.
